summary: Weekly POC check-in focused on latency tuning. Covered recent benchmark results (TTFT improvements with streaming), kernel selection tradeoffs for 4k vs 8k sequences, and next steps to run end-to-end TTFT tests in customer's staging network and prepare canary config for dedicated pool.
transcript: 00:00 - Meeting header: 2027-03-11 14:00 PDT | Duration: ~45m | Attendees: Sofia, Diego (Redwood); Marta, Ethan, Priya, Jonas (Crestline)
00:12 - Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check: same agenda as last week, run through results, dig into TTFT and streaming, and decide next experiments?
00:28 - Marta: Yep that's right. We want to see where we can shave latency before we consider a canary in dedicated. Primary KPI is median TTFT under 250ms for short prompts.
00:45 - Diego: Great. Quick context — last week's runs showed median TTFT ~310ms on the hosted config with non-streaming, we enabled async batching and KV cache but still saw spikes at tail.
01:12 - Ethan: Right, our internal SLA target is 250ms median and 500ms p95. We observed p95 around 680ms with some big sequence requests making the tail worse.

01:40 - Diego: So the two levers we tested: enabling streaming (chunked token delivery) and using kernel variants optimized for longer sequences. With streaming on, TTFT dropped ~80-90ms in our infra tests.
02:05 - Priya: Just to clarify — by streaming you mean server-side streaming (chunked HTTP) so client gets first token faster, correct? We need to confirm our client stack handles partial responses.

02:22 - Sofia: Exactly. Streaming reduces perceived latency because the client shows first token earlier, even if overall completion is same. For some use-cases first token is crucial, like chat UI impressions.
03:00 - Ethan: Any tradeoffs on token quality or ordering when streaming is enabled? We had a previous concern about early stopping or hallucinations if the client interrupts the stream.

03:18 - Diego: Good point. Functionally there's no quality change from Redwood's side; streaming just flushes generation as it's produced. If client cancels mid-generation you get partial output — needs client logic to retry or call continuation endpoint.
04:05 - Marta: Can you walk through kernel choices? Last note from SE was that 'standard' kernel vs 'fused-attn' or some vendor-specific kernel impacted long-sequence perf.

04:30 - Diego: Sure. For 4k sequences the fused-attn kernel gives better throughput and slightly lower latency for longer contexts; for 8k we switch to a different kernel path that trades a bit of startup cost for amortized per-token speed. There's also quantization impacts — int8 vs int4 profiles differed by ~5-10% latency and larger impact on memory.
05:05 - Jonas: So for our mix (70% short prompts, 30% long multi-turn) would you recommend a single kernel or dynamic routing?

05:20 - Diego: Dynamic routing is the sweet spot — route short requests to low-latency kernel and longer contexts to the high-throughput kernel. Redwood can set routing rules by sequence length and fall back when capacity is constrained.
06:02 - Priya: Are there any implications for KV cache when switching kernels? We store long conversation prefixes in cache and worried about cache compatibility across kernel variants.

06:20 - Diego: We keep KV cache format compatible across the runtime; switching kernels is transparent. The main caution is warm vs cold cache — if a request misses cache you'll see a bigger TTFT hit. Prefetching common prefixes helps.
07:00 - Ethan: Diego earlier mentioned batching; how aggressive are you batching in hosted vs dedicated? Batching helps cost but could hurt TTFT.

07:20 - Diego: Right — continuous batching waits a small window to aggregate tokens. We tune batch windows aggressively for low-latency workloads (10-20ms). For ultra-low TTFT we can disable batching for short requests or route them to a dedicated low-latency pool.

08:05 - Sofia: Today we ran three test vectors: 1) baseline hosted non-streaming, 2) hosted with streaming enabled, 3) hosted with streaming + kernel hint for short sequences. Diego, can you summarize numbers?

08:25 - Diego: Baseline median TTFT 310ms, stream-only median 240ms, stream+kernel-hint median 225ms. p95 improved from 680ms to 420ms with streaming, and to ~380ms with the kernel hint. These were on Redwood's test harness with mock egress — we need to run in Crestline staging network to validate end-to-end.
09:10 - Marta: Those are promising. Any differences in token cost or resource usage with streaming?

09:25 - Diego: Streaming itself doesn't change token compute; cost is largely unchanged. The kernel choices can slightly change per-token time which affects throughput and cost; fused kernels are slightly more efficient so cost per token goes down marginally.
10:00 - Priya: For the staging tests we need to replicate network conditions — our staging has a 20-30ms egress to Redwood's region and occasional packet loss. Would that invalidate the numbers?

10:20 - Diego: Network latency adds directly to TTFT for first token. If your egress is 25ms RTT that adds ~25ms per roundtrip. Streaming reduces the need for multiple roundtrips before first token, so it's actually more robust under higher RTT.
11:05 - Ethan: What about quantization? Last week we tried int8 which lowered memory but we saw slight jitter in latencies.

11:20 - Diego: Quantization profiles trade precision for memory and can affect kernel selection. int8 gave consistent speedups for throughput but sometimes increased tail variance. For strict latency SLOs we recommended int8 with conservative fallback to float16 for problematic prompts.

12:00 - Sofia: Let's discuss concrete experiments to run before next week: Diego will run the TTFT+streaming benchmark in Crestline staging (with real network), run sequence-length routing test, and measure p50/p95/p99. Marta/Priya will enable VPC peering in staging so we can run end-to-end; Ethan will provide top-100 prompts to seed cache.
12:38 - Marta: Sounds good. One more question — if we move to Dedicated pool, will we be able to pin kernel variants for that pool?

12:50 - Diego: Yes, Dedicated allows more control — you can pin kernel profile, quantization, and autoscale policies. We can propose a canary config that pins low-latency kernel for short-request nodes and high-throughput for other nodes.
13:20 - Jonas: On governance / compliance note, do you have audit logs for model invocations? We'll need that for our risk team before go-live.
13:35 - Sofia: Yes — Redwood Private and Dedicated include request-level audit logs, KMS integration, and SOC2 artifacts. I'll attach the security pack after the call.

14:05 - Ethan: Operationally, if streaming works well, client changes are minimal? We currently poll for full response; switching to streaming means changing the client to render partial tokens and handle interrupts.
14:25 - Sofia: We'll share a quick snippet for JS and Python streaming clients. Diego: toss in guidance on retry logic for aborted streams.
14:45 - Diego: Will do. Also I'll include the exact kernel flags we used in the experiments and the perf spreadsheet with raw logs.

15:10 - Sofia: Recap / next steps: Diego runs staging TTFT + streaming tests (due 3/15), Priya shares infra diagram and enables peering (due 3/13), Sofia sends pricing and security pack (due 3/12), Ethan shares prompt samples (due 3/14). We'll reconvene same time next week to review results.
15:35 - Marta: Thanks everyone, that covers it. Meeting end.
15:40 - End of transcript
